name: Dataproc
oneLiner: Managed Spark and Hadoop for batch, streaming and ML workloads.
whatItIs: Dataproc is Google Cloud's managed Spark and Hadoop service. It runs the open-source big-data stack (Spark, Hadoop, Hive, Presto, Flink) on clusters GCP provisions in around 90 seconds — famously fast — so the cloud-native pattern is to create a cluster per job, run it, and delete it. Data lives in Cloud Storage rather than cluster HDFS, making clusters disposable compute. There's also Dataproc Serverless, where you submit a Spark job and skip cluster management entirely. It's the choice when you want real Spark control on GCP rather than the fully-abstracted Dataflow.

inPractice.narrative: A team has existing PySpark jobs and terabytes of data in Cloud Storage. They submit each job to Dataproc Serverless (or spin up an ephemeral cluster), which reads from GCS, processes at scale, and writes curated Parquet back to GCS. BigQuery then queries the results. Dataproc is picked over Dataflow when the team already has Spark/Hadoop code and wants to run it as-is with full control.

coreConcepts.detail: Clusters start in ~90 seconds, so the norm is job-scoped clusters: create, run, delete. You don't pay for idle infrastructure between jobs.
Submit a Spark batch or session without creating a cluster; GCP sizes and runs it, billing for what the job uses — the no-ops option.
Data sits in Cloud Storage (via the connector), not cluster HDFS, so clusters are disposable and multiple jobs share the same data.
Runs Spark, Hadoop, Hive, Presto/Trino, Flink and more with chosen versions and optional components/initialization actions for custom setup.
Clusters can autoscale, and using preemptible (Spot) secondary workers cuts cost significantly for fault-tolerant batch work.
Define a sequence of jobs (optionally on a managed ephemeral cluster) that Dataproc runs and cleans up — lightweight pipeline orchestration.

whenToUse: Running existing Spark/Hadoop/Hive code on GCP with minimal changes.
Code-first big-data processing where you want cluster/version control.
Ephemeral, per-job clusters or serverless Spark to avoid idle cost.
Cost-optimised batch via preemptible VMs and autoscaling.
Migrating on-prem Hadoop/Spark to managed GCP.
whenNotToUse: Fully-managed, autoscaling streaming pipelines with no infra thought — Dataflow fits better.
Pure SQL analytics — do it in BigQuery.
Teams wanting zero Spark/Hadoop knowledge — Dataflow/BigQuery abstract more.
Tiny occasional tasks — a Cloud Function or BigQuery job may be simpler.

keyFacts.label: Frameworks
keyFacts.value: Spark, Hadoop, Hive, Presto/Trino, Flink, etc.

keyFacts.label: Cluster start
keyFacts.value: ~90 seconds — designed for ephemeral, per-job clusters.

keyFacts.label: Serverless
keyFacts.value: Dataproc Serverless runs Spark with no cluster to manage.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Compute Engine resources + small per-vCPU Dataproc premium (or Serverless per-usage).

pricingShape: For clusters you pay for the underlying Compute Engine VMs plus a small Dataproc premium per vCPU while the cluster runs — so ephemeral clusters and preemptible workers keep costs low, and a forgotten running cluster is the main waste. Dataproc Serverless bills for the resources a job consumes with nothing idle. Storage is separate in Cloud Storage. Because clusters spin up so fast, the disciplined pattern (one cluster per job, deleted after) is easy and cheap; long-lived clusters only make sense for steady interactive use.
gotchas: A long-running cluster left up costs money for nothing — prefer ephemeral or serverless.
Preemptible workers can vanish mid-job; keep primary workers non-preemptible and design for retries.
It's real Spark — you own tuning and version choices; defaults aren't optimal for large jobs.
The GCS connector isn't HDFS; some Hadoop assumptions (rename atomicity, small-file performance) differ.
Choosing Dataproc when Dataflow's managed model would fit adds ops burden you didn't need.
